sections.html:
This Pee Dee county covers about 937 square miles, almost entirely land. Kingstree serves as county seat and largest community, with Andrews, Greeleyville, Hemingway, Lane and Stuckey nearby. Most residents, about 83 percent, live in rural areas, which means plenty of sellers hold large lots, farm parcels or mobile homes on land they own.

Population fell from 37,217 in 2000 to 31,026 at the 2020 census, and Kingstree itself held 3,244. Manufacturing supplies the largest share of jobs, at about 30.2 percent, with public administration, retail and health care behind it. Interstates 20, 26 and 95 connect the county to larger southeastern cities.

Homes left by a parent and never retitled turn up often. Estate papers will be requested before a deed can go on record.

Ground along the Black River can flood in a big storm, so check the flood zone before marketing a home. Hurricane Matthew in October 2016 dropped close to 10 inches of rain on parts of the county, with one gauge northwest of Kingstree reading 13.70 inches.

Storm damage makes conventional financing difficult. Selling for cash in present condition is an option for owners who can't pay for repairs.

Your bill passes through four hands: the assessor values the property, the auditor applies the millage, the treasurer collects payment, and the delinquent tax collector steps in after March 16. All four answer at the county switchboard, (843) 355-9321.

OfficeExtensionMailing address
Assessor5500PO Box 330, Kingstree, SC 29556
Auditor5600PO Box 7, Kingstree, SC 29556
Treasurer5900PO Box 150, Kingstree, SC 29556
Delinquent tax collector5800PO Box 477, Kingstree, SC 29556

Both the treasurer and the delinquent office are at 201 W Main Street, Kingstree, open 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday to Friday, holidays excluded. The delinquent office doesn't take American Express or Discover and won't accept payment on bills that aren't delinquent yet. Not sure where deeds are recorded? Ask the treasurer's staff.

Pay by January 15 and nothing extra is added. Miss it and 3 percent goes on the bill. From February 2 through March 16, another 7 percent is stacked on top. On March 17 the account moves to the delinquent tax collector, where unpaid real property and mobile home bills go into execution, and state law attaches a final 5 percent.

The 3 percent step begins on whichever comes later: January 16, or thirty days after the notices were mailed. That gives some relief when the county mails late.

Fair market value is multiplied by 4 percent for the home you live in and by 6 percent for most everything else. If you inherit a house, move out and rent it, expect the higher rate and a larger bill. Vacant lots are in the 6 percent group as well.

Values are redone every five years, though an ordinance can let a county hold the new numbers back for one tax year. You should hear from the county whenever your value or classification shifts by $1,000 or more.

Disputes move through four stages, and each has its own deadline:

  1. A written objection to the assessor, within 90 days of the mailing date on the notice.
  2. A written protest, within 30 days after you meet with the assessor.
  3. An appeal to the county board of assessment appeals, within 30 days of the assessor's reply.
  4. A hearing request to the Administrative Law Court, within 30 days of the board's written ruling.

No notice came this year? You may still object in writing, and one filed ahead of the first penalty date applies to that year's bill.

The path from a late bill to a lost house is slow, and it has several warning points. Around April 1 the officer mails a delinquent notice to the taxpayer and anyone who holds the land by grant. If 30 days pass with no payment, the officer seizes the real property by certified mail. Then the property is advertised as a Delinquent Tax Sale, once weekly for three weeks, before it is sold.

Even after the sale you have twelve months to get it back. The owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem. The price is the bid plus interest on it that grows by quarter: 3 percent in months one through three, then 6, 9 and 12 percent. About 20 to 45 days before the window closes, the collector mails a certified notice. For this year's sale schedule and fee amounts, call extension 5800.

Rural parcels bring their own questions. A mobile home on the land is billed under the same schedule as the land. Pull every tax notice for the property, not just the one for the house, and confirm that each is paid or accounted for.

If a family farm parcel passed down without a clean title, start the estate paperwork early, since the deed can't be recorded until it is sorted. Walk the boundaries with someone who knows them, note anything that floods near the Black River, and write down repairs you won't make. A buyer who knows these facts up front is far less likely to renegotiate later.

Recording a deed runs $1.85 for every $500 of value, or part of $500, and by default the seller pays. The state keeps $1.30 and the county gets $0.55.

An affidavit has to go with the deed, either stating what the property is worth or explaining why the deed is exempt. Transfers of $100 or less and deeds in lieu of foreclosure are exempt. Lying on the affidavit is a misdemeanor.

Nothing says you must clear the bill before you sell. The closing attorney requests a payoff from the treasurer or the delinquent office and takes that amount out of your proceeds, so a sale ahead of a tax sale can wipe out the debt.

Ask for the payoff on paper, with penalties and costs included, and find out how many days it holds. Inherited houses call for a death certificate and any probate papers. Mention a mobile home on the land to the buyer, because its tax runs on the same schedule. When a tax sale has already taken place, the twelve months to redeem count from the sale date.

If you are short on time, a cash offer avoids waiting on a buyer's loan approval. We buy Williamsburg County houses as-is, so send the address along with the amount owed.

faqs.q: What is the Williamsburg County property tax due date?
faqs.a: Payment is penalty-free through January 15. A 3 percent charge follows, with another 7 percent from February 2 through March 16.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Williamsburg County property tax?
faqs.a: Call (843) 355-9321 and ask for extension 5900 for the treasurer, 5600 for the auditor, 5500 for the assessor or 5800 for the delinquent tax collector.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Williamsburg County assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days, counted from the mailing date of the assessor's notice, to file a written objection. Each later step has a 30 day limit.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Williamsburg County house if the tax is delinquent?
faqs.a: Yes, and the balance usually comes out of the proceeds at closing. First obtain a written payoff from the delinquent tax office so it covers penalties and costs.

faqs.q: Can I get my house back after a Williamsburg County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, if you act inside twelve months. Redeeming means paying the winning bid plus 3, 6, 9 or 12 percent interest, depending on the quarter. A grantee or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem too.
